opus-5.5.text:
I think the bar for success isn't really a robot that can do one impressive trick, like folding a shirt perfectly in a lab. It's something more like a robot that you can bring into your home and give fairly open-ended instructions to, and it just figures things out in the way a reasonable person would. So, you say "clean up the kitchen," and it understands that means putting the dishes in the dishwasher, wiping down the counter, maybe noticing the milk was left out and putting it back in the fridge, without you having to spell out every step.

And critically, it should be able to do that in *your* kitchen, not one it was trained in. Every home is different: different layouts, different objects, different ways people like things done. So a big part of autonomy is generalization, being able to handle the long tail of situations it's never seen before, and recovering gracefully when something goes wrong. If it drops a cup, it should pick it up. If a drawer is stuck, it should try something else instead of just freezing.

The other piece, which I think people underappreciate, is that it should get better over time. A truly successful system wouldn't be static. It would learn from its own experience in your home, learn your preferences, and keep improving, much like a person who starts a new job is a bit clumsy on day one but is competent a few weeks in. To me, that combination of broad generalization, robustness, and continual improvement through experience is what real autonomy would look like. And I think we're actually closer to that than many people assume, because the foundation-model approach gives us that general prior. The remaining question is how to get these systems to practice and learn on their own in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes open-ended household instructions, inferring the steps for chores without spelling out every action, and learning the household’s preferences.

r002.rationale: It gives no intended task duration of months to a year.

r003.rationale: It does not say the robot should independently seek missing information needed to fulfill a request.

r004.rationale: It describes recovering from problems such as a dropped cup or stuck drawer, but does not state that the robot should recognize exceptional cases requiring more deliberate reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that I would want to see is not really a specific task, it's more a kind of robustness and a kind of generality that we currently don't have. So let me try to unpack that a little bit.

If you think about what makes a household environment hard, it's not that any one thing is especially difficult. Loading a dishwasher is not, in principle, a very complicated motor skill. The problem is that every house is different, every dish is different, the dishwasher is in a different place, somebody left a pot in the sink that's half full of water, the lighting is weird because it's evening. And so what you really need is a system that, when it encounters a situation that it hasn't seen before, can figure out what to do in a sensible way. It can fall back on some kind of common sense.

And I think the honest answer is that for a long time in robotics we kind of avoided that problem. We would set up a demo where the robot does one thing in one environment, and it looks great, and then you move the table six inches and it falls apart. So to me successful autonomy looks like: you take the robot to a home it's never been in, you tell it in plain language what you want, and it just does it. And if something goes wrong, it notices and recovers, or it asks you, rather than confidently doing the wrong thing. That last part is actually really important. A robot that is right ninety-five percent of the time and catastrophically wrong five percent of the time is not a robot you want in your kitchen.

The other thing I would add is that I think the bar for "successful" should be that it improves with use. Right now most robots are kind of frozen. You deploy them and they're as good as they'll ever be. But a household is a place where the robot is going to be living, essentially, for years. It should be learning about your house, learning your preferences, learning that you like the mugs on the second shelf. That's where the learning-based approach really pays off, because the data is just there, it's being generated every day, and the robot that doesn't use it is leaving a lot on the table.

So I guess the short version is: generality to handle the long tail, enough judgment to know when it's out of its depth, and the ability to get better over time. If we had those three things, I think the specific tasks would mostly take care of themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot should learn household preferences, but it does not frame autonomy as following standing preferences instead of requiring a separate command for each chore.

r002.rationale: It says the robot may live in a household for years, but gives no months-to-a-year duration for a household task.

r003.rationale: The robot may ask the user when something goes wrong, but the response does not say it should independently seek missing information needed to fulfill a request.

r004.rationale: The response says the robot should notice when it is out of its depth and recover or ask, but does not state that it should recognize exceptional cases requiring more deliberate reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you can give it an objective without having to specify every step. You say, “Could you clean up the kitchen?” and it figures out what needs to be put away, what needs to be washed, and where things belong. If it opens the dishwasher and discovers that it’s full of clean dishes, it understands that it needs to unload those first.

The interesting part is what happens when something doesn’t go according to plan. It drops a utensil, or there’s an object it hasn’t seen before. Can it recover? Can it recognize when it should ask you a question? You don’t want a robot that needs supervision every thirty seconds, but you also don’t want one that confidently makes irreversible mistakes.

So I would measure success by how much responsibility you can actually delegate to it. Can you go do something else and reasonably expect that, when you come back, the kitchen will be clean? That requires a whole collection of capabilities working together over a long period, rather than just a really impressive demonstration of one manipulation skill.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving the robot a specific objective such as cleaning the kitchen; it does not frame autonomy as following standing household preferences instead of receiving a separate command for each chore.

r002.rationale: It discusses completing a kitchen-cleaning task over a long period, but gives no intended duration of months to a year.

r003.rationale: It says the robot should recognize when to ask a question, but does not state that it should independently seek missing information needed to fulfill the request.

r004.rationale: It describes recovering from dropped or unfamiliar objects, but does not say the robot should recognize exceptional cases that require more deliberate reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the real test is whether the robot can take responsibility for a task without you having to specify every step. You could say, “Can you get the kitchen ready for dinner?” and it would figure out what needs to be put away, what needs to be cleaned, and where things belong. If something unexpected happens, it can recover, or ask you a useful question and then continue.

There’s a big difference between a robot that can demonstrate each of those behaviors and one that you can actually depend on. If you have to supervise it constantly, you’ve become the robot’s caretaker. Successful autonomy would mean it saves you attention as well as physical effort. You can go do something else and trust that it will either finish the job or let you know when it needs help.

r003.rationale: It says the robot may ask a useful question when something unexpected happens, but does not clearly state that it should independently seek missing information needed to fulfill a request.
